d: A low bed to be slid under a higher bed
ety: From Middle English trondlin, trondelen, a variation of Middle English trendlen, from Old English trendlian. More at trendle, trindle.
s: He could hear the trundle of cart wheels.

d: Arrived at without due care or effort; lacking depth
ety: Borrowed from Middle French facile, from Latin facilis (“easy to do, easy, doable”), from Latin facere (“to do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put”) Compare Spanish and Portuguese fácil (“easy”), Catalan fàcil, Romanian facil. First use appears c. 1484 in a translation by William Caxton.
s: Her writing was facile and articulate.

d: A flamboyant deceiver; one who attracts customers with tricks or jokes
ety: From Middle French charlatan, from Old Italian ciarlatano (“quack”), a blend of ciarlatore (“chatterer”) + cerretano (“hawker, quack”, literally “native of Cerreto”) (Cerreto di Spoleto being a village in Umbria, known for its quacks).
s: That this disgraceful charlatan holds one of the great offices of state in this country should be a source of constant shame and embarrassment to the Prime Minister.

d: Servile flattery; exaggerated and hypocritical praise
ety: From French adulation, from Latin adulātio (“flattery”).
s: He was uncomfortable with the adulation from his fans.

d: Eager to surpass others
ety: From rivalry + -ous.
s: Western universalism was real, if rivalrous.

d: Abusive or venomous language used to express blame or censure or bitter deep-seated ill will
ety: From Middle French invective, from Medieval Latin invectiva (“abusive speech”), from Latin invectīvus, from invectus, perfect passive participle of invehō (“bring in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”). See vehicle, and compare with inveigh.
s: Politics can raise invective to a low art.

d: Take in, also metaphorically
ety: From Middle English imbiben, from Latin imbibō, from im- + bibō (“to drink”) (whence also beverage), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃-, whence also potable, potion.
s: Like the late Dr Falk (d. 1782), Grabianka was a native of Podolia, where Sabbatian influences were strong among local Jews, and he imbibed many of their notions.

d: Impossible to subdue
ety: From Late Latin indomitābilis, from in- (“not”) + domitō, frequentative of domō (“to tame”). By surface analysis, in- + domitable.
s: But he was a youth of indomitable spirit, strong and agile as a wild cat.

d: Inclined to a healthy reddish color often associated with outdoor life
ety: From Latin rubicundus, from rubere (“to be red”).
s: He was of a full, rubicund countenance, with a double chin, aquiline nose, and a pleasant twinkling eye.

d: A melodic phrase that accompanies the reappearance of a person or situation (as in Wagner’s operas)
ety: From German Leitmotiv (“leading motif”), from leiten (“to lead”) + Motiv (“motif”), originally used to describe Wagnerian opera. The spelling was influenced by motif.
s: If one looks for a pattern in the political life of John Connally, one finds a leitmotif of scandals which threatened but never destroyed his career.

d: A conversation especially a formal one
ety: From Middle English colloquies pl, from Latin colloquium (“conversation”), from com- (“together, with”) (English com-) + form of loquor (“speak”) (from which English locution and other words). Doublet of colloquium.
s: At the end of the colloquy, Judge Spicer asked Carr whether anyone had "pressured" him into accepting the deal.

d: An oppressively hot southerly wind from the Sahara that blows across Egypt in the spring
ety: From Egyptian Arabic خَمْسِين (ḵamsīn, “fifty”); see khamaseen for more.
s: That second spring the khamseen was worse than I have ever known it before or since.

d: Apathy and inactivity in the practice of virtue (personified as one of the deadly sins)
ety: Borrowed from Latin acēdia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀκηδίᾱ (akēdíā), from ἀκηδής (akēdḗs, “careless”) + -ίᾱ (-íā). Doublet of accidie.
s: Her acedia kept her trapped in a cycle of depression and torpor.

d: Harsh or corrosive in tone
ety: From vitriol + -ic; or from French vitriolique (cognate with Italian vetriolico, Portuguese vitriolico, Spanish vitriólico).
s: You vitriolic, patriotic, slam fight, bright light / Feeling pretty psyched

d: Repetitive nonmeaningful speech (especially that associated with a trance state or religious fervor)
ety: From glosso- + -lalia, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă, “tongue; language”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *glōgʰs) + λᾰλῐᾱ́ (lălĭā́, “talking; form of speech, dialect”) (from λᾰ́λος (lắlos, “talkative”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming feminine abstract nouns)).
s: Everything was a labyrinthine amalgam of languages, a towering Babel of puns and glossolalia.

d: Straying from the right course or from accepted standards
ety: From Middle English erraunt [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman erraunt, from Old French errant, the present participle of errer (“to walk (to); to wander (to); (figuratively) to travel, voyage”), and then: * from Vulgar Latin iterāre (compare Late Latin itinerāre, itinerāri (“to travel, voyage”)), from Latin iter (“a route (including a journey, trip; a course; a path; a road)”), ultimately from
s: We ran down the street in pursuit of the errant dog.

d: The person for whom something is named
ety: From Latin eponymus, from Ancient Greek ἐπώνῠμος (epṓnŭmos), from ἐπί (epí, “upon, epi-”) + ὄνυμα (ónuma, “name”) + -ος (-os, suffix forming adjectives and nouns). Equivalent to epi- + -nym.
s: Rockefeller became the very eponym of wealth.

d: Involving clever rogues or adventurers especially as in a type of fiction
ety: From picaro (“adventurer, rogue”) + -esque (suffix meaning ‘in the style or manner of’ forming adjectives), modelled after Spanish picaresco (“in the style or manner of a picaro; picaresque”), from pícaro (“rogue”) + -esco (suffix forming adjectives indicating a relation). Compare French picaresque (attested later than the English word), Italian picaresco, Portuguese picaresco.
s: Spain became celebrated about the end of this century for her novels in the picaresque style, of which Lazarillo de Tormes is the oldest extant specimen.

d: The reestablishing of cordial relations
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French rapprochement (“act or process of getting closer together; link (between two things)”).
s: It was the Nixon administration that saw the rapprochement between the United States and China.

d: Someone who drives a herd
ety: From drove + -er.
s: In the present day, we take it for granted that livestock are transported by truck or rail, but in past centuries, they were driven by drovers, and a herd might be met on any street, road, or highway.

d: Give new life or energy to
ety: Partly from French revivifier and partly from Latin revīvificō, corresponding to re- + vivify.
s: A hot soup will revive me.

d: Submissive or fawning in attitude or behavior
ety: From Middle English servyle, from Old French servil, servile, from Latin servīlis, from servus (“slave”). By surface analysis, serve + -ile.
s: Even fortune rules no more, O servile land!

d: A low transparent cover put over young plants to protect them from cold
ety: Borrowed from French cloche (“bell”), from Medieval Latin clocca (“bell”). Doublet of cloak and clock.
s: Pistachio and date-filled cakes glisten under a glass cloche as customers drinking cardamom tea settle into brightly tapestried pouf chairs at the Pouya café and cultural center in Paris.

d: A painting or carving (especially an altarpiece) on two panels (usually hinged like a book)
ety: From Late Latin diptycha, plural, from Ancient Greek, neuter plural of δίπτυχος (díptukhos, “folded, doubled”), from δι- (di-) + πτυχή (ptukhḗ, “fold, layer”).
s: “Vegetation of the Sonoran Desert” is the first volume of a diptych “Vegetation and Flora of the Sonoran Desert,” for which Ira L. Wiggins is to write the companion volume on the flora.

d: Sound practical judgment
ety: Borrowed from Scots gumption (“common sense, shrewdness; drive, initiative”); further etymology unknown, possibly connected with Middle English gome (“attention, heed”), from Old Norse gaumr (“attention, heed”), from Proto-Germanic *gaumō. English cognates include gaum (“to comprehend, understand”) and goam (“to recognize, see”).
s: Whatever the job turned out to be, if it went against her gumptions, she would make sure Gregory would have hell on his hands and make him eager to release her from the deal.

d: Ludicrous or incongruous unnaturalness or distortion
ety: From French grotesquerie, from grotesque (“farcical, grotesque”) + -erie (“-ery”), from Italian grottesco, from grotta (“cave, grotto”) + -esco (“-esque, -ish”). Equivalent to grotesque + -erie.
s: The tone is brittle and morbid, emphasizing the eerie grotesquerie of Albert Giraud's poems.

d: An informal conversation
ety: From Middle English confabulacion (“conversation”), from Latin confābulātiōnem, from cōnfābulārī + -tiōnem.
s: Segal said another characteristic of Trump’s questionable mental acuity is confabulation. “It’s where he takes an idea or something that’s happened and he adds to it things that have not happened.”

d: Effusively or insincerely emotional
ety: From Middle English Maudelen, a dialectal form of Mary Magdalene (typically depicted weeping), from Old French Madelaine (whence Madeleine), from Late Latin Magdalena (see Magdalena, Magdalene, and Maudlin).
s: He was a drunkard, and had not known it. What he had fondly imagined was a pleasant exhilaration had been maudlin intoxication.

d: Marked by obliqueness or indirection in speech or conduct
ety: First attested in 1664. From Latin circuitōsus, from circuitus, from circumeō (“to go around”), from circum (“around”) + eō (“to go”). By surface analysis, circuit + -ous.
s: The explanation was circuitous and puzzling.

d: Conformity with some esthetic standard of correctness or propriety
ety: From Middle English nicetee, from Old French niceté (“simpleness, foolishness”), from nice (“simple, foolish”); equivalent to nice + -e- + -ty.
s: A rocket-propelled grenade doesn't have the nicety of a sniper round, but you must admit its effectiveness.

d: Having many aspects
ety: From Latin multifārius.
s: It is divided into parts that are too small and multifarious.

d: A person who is rejected (from society or home)
ety: From Tamil பறையர் (paṟaiyar), from பறையன் (paṟaiyaṉ, “drummer”), from பறை (paṟai, “drum”) or from Malayalam പറയർ (paṟayaṟ), from പറയൻ (paṟayaṉ, “drummer”), from പറ (paṟa, “drum”). Parai in Tamil or Para in Malayalam refers to a type of large drum designed to announce the king’s notices to the public. The people who made a living using the parai were called paraiyar; in the caste-based society, the
s: I’m a pariah, outlawed from Time Lord society.

d: A representation of a person (especially in the form of sculpture)
ety: From French effigie, from Latin effigiēs (“likeness, effigy”), from effingō (“represent, portray”).
s: In England on Bonfire Night, an effigy is often burned.

d: Something intended to misrepresent the true nature of an activity
ety: Borrowed from Middle French subterfuge m, from Medieval Latin subterfugium n, from Latin subterfugiō (“to flee secretly”), from subter (“under”) and fugiō (“to flee”).
s: Overt subterfuge in a region nearly caused a minor accident.

d: Excessively or hypocritically pious
ety: From sanctimony + -ous.
s: Thou conclud'st like the sanctimonious pirate, that went to sea with the Ten Commandements, but scrap'd one out of the table.

d: A report (often malicious) about the behavior of other people
ety: The noun is derived from scuttle (“to cut a hole through (something)”) + butt (“wooden cask”). Noun sense 2 (“gossip, idle chatter; rumour”) refers to the fact that sailors would gather around the scuttlebutt to drink and exchange gossip; compare furphy and water cooler. The verb is derived from the noun.
s: His resolve not to worry about unfounded scuttlebutt lasted about two minutes.

d: An authoritative declaration
ety: From Latin dictum (“proverb, maxim”), from dictus (“having been said”), perfect passive participle of dico (“to say”). Compare Spanish dicho (“saying”). Doublet of dict.
s: 1. The utmost in steam producing capacity permitted by weight and dimensions; in other words, capacity to boil water—H. A. Ivatt's old dictum.

d: Marked by a ready flow of speech
ety: From Middle French volubile, from Latin volūbilis (“rolling”), from volvō (“roll”).
s: What fun shone in his eyes as he recalled some of her fine speeches, and repeated them, imitating her voluble delivery!

d: A stipulated condition
ety: Borrowed from Latin proviso (“it being provided”), ablative singular neuter of provisus, past participle of providere (“to provide”); see provide.
s: The writing has been on the wall that Americans’ support for mass deportation was subject to all kinds of caveats and provisos.

d: Deeply or seriously thoughtful
ety: From ruminate + -ive.
s: They waited expectantly while he directed a ruminative yawn toward the white smiling moon.
